comment:
I am writing in support of CMS’ proposals to improve interoperability and streamline electronic prior authorization. The agency’s proposal will help to relieve the immense burden prior authorization has placed on me and other providers. It is critical that CMS finalize the proposed rule to mitigate the unwarranted burden prior authorization has been on both patients and providers. I also encourage CMS to do more to address this issue.

While I support CMS’ efforts overall, I urge the agency to see how arbitrary denials have a direct impact on the quality and overall benefits of essential medical services provided by physical therapists. PTs and other providers are continually experiencing more demanding, complicated, and burdensome utilization reduction polices. Often, my patients must postpone care due to seemingly arbitrary denials, which are overturned on appeal but at considerable time and expense to the provider; delays in making a determination; piecemeal approvals requiring the provider to repeatedly resubmit the same requests; and payment denials for lack of authorization even when it was properly obtained.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly patients and providers must be able to appeal any modification the payer makes to the request if they feel it was made in error.

I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, and the patient’s prior authorization decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. Additionally, a study from HHS’ Office of the Inspector General found that capitated payment models such as those under MA can encourage MAOs to deny prior authorization claims, including claims that would otherwise not be denied under traditional Medicare. My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care.

comment:
Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:

I am a Patient Service Coordinator at a physical therapy private practice who has 2 years of experience providing services to Medicare patients. For these patients, delays in care or denial of medically necessary services means poorer outcomes. For providers like ours, avoidable administrative burden means that instead of providing care to patients, we are spending time and resources on inefficient paperwork.

I want to thank CMS for its proposal to streamline administrative burden by establishing an automated prior authorization process. Reducing the number of times and how long it will take to process authorization requests is a welcome change. The proposed changes will address avoidable delays in patient care, achieve better health outcomes, and improve the care experience across providers, patients, and caregivers by significantly reducing wait times and increasing transparency around decisions.

In my experience, delays in care means that patients either don’t achieve optimal outcomes or it takes more visits overall; either of those options ends up costing the system more money. Last year we had to wait an average of 7 days before I got authorization to proceed for patients covered by MA plans. The changes you are proposing will make a big difference to both our ability to provide timely patient care and save both time and money.

Thank you for taking my perspective into consideration as you craft regulations which could make a big impact on how readily my patients can access care—which will also impact how quickly we can help restore their function and reduce their pain.

Thank you,


Shannon Garvey, Patient Service Coordinator
Asis Physical Therapy

comment: I am the utilization manager at a Certified Community Behavioral Health Center in Missouri and have managed prior authorizations for outpatient psychotherapy and medication services.  Speaking strictly in the context of BH prior authorizations I have found that the requirements have varied every year for the last 20 years with the changes being related to the cost of the administrative burden and not anything to do with patient care and treatment.  1. Prior authorization is rarely, if ever, denied.  Providers are careful to provide medically necessary treatment and have enough clients that extending therapy is simply not necessary.  We are bound by ethical guidelines and take pride in providing competent services. 2. There is not a consistent application of guidelines related to number of sessions, types of sessions, etc. Since therapy is very dependent upon the individual's situation there is no one size fits all.  3.  Application process can be overly simplistic meaning it has no purpose, to overly burdensome which casts doubt if the information requested is valid for this purpose.  4. It limits patient self-determination as most carriers only provide auths for one provider or provider group.  So if the individual wants to seek services at more than one location, they can't.  5.  Any money saved by limiting services is lost due to the administrative burden of maintaining prior authorizations.  This can cause providers to lose money and thus clients losing services.  6. In my experience all carriers have tried this at least once and most have ceased after their first year.  All have stated it was due to the administrative burden.  The only carrier that seems to require prior authorizations is the state Medicaid program.  Which, as we all know, can't hardly keep up with the re-certification process which is coming due again due to the unwinding of the PHE rules.

comment:
Re: Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes for Medicare Advantage Organizations (MA) and Medicaid Managed Care Plans..., (CMS-0057-P)

The ALS Association appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Center for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule, “Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes for MA Organizations and Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, State CHIP Agencies, CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of QHPs in the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges.”

Our comments are specifically focused on the proposed rule as it pertains to ensuring access to essential health care for people living with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) who are enrolled in Medicare Advantage (MA) plans. We strongly support provisions of the proposed rule that would improve prior authorization processes to better ensure timely access to needed items and services for patients and reduce burden on providers. We thank CMS for its work – through this proposed rule and other actions including proposals in the CY 2024 MA and Part D Proposed Rule – to advance these goals and ensure equal access to covered services for both MA and Traditional Medicare enrollees.

Please see attached letter to reference The ALS Association comments in full.

comment:
Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:
The Alliance for Nursing Informatics (ANI) appreciates the opportunity to comment as nursing stakeholders to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Request for Information: Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes Proposed Rule.
The Alliance for Nursing Informatics (ANI), cosponsored by AMIA and HIMSS, advances nursing informatics leadership, practice, education, policy, and research through a unified voice of nursing informatics organizations. We transform health and healthcare through nursing informatics and innovation. ANI is a collaboration of organizations representing more than 20,000 nurse informaticists and bringing together 25 distinct nursing informatics groups globally. ANI crosses academia, practice, industry, and nursing specialty boundaries and collaborates with the more than 4 million nurses in practice today.
The nursing workforce is under tremendous strain. Nurses are experiencing burnout due to a myriad of factors impacting nurses’ well-being, one of which is the technological stress of electronic health record (EHR) documentation requirements. As a matter of principle, ANI is in favor of electronically optimizing healthcare processes and enhancing interoperability in a manner that puts the needs of the patient first. We are supporters of the “Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act” and have commented on CMS Promoting Interoperability and Electronic Healthcare Information Exchange, Patients Over Paperwork, and other CMS initiatives over the years. We strive to ensure that health IT tools are leveraged appropriately to make healthcare documentation processes, including prior authorization, more efficient for patients, providers and payers, across diverse settings and use cases.
However, ANI remains concerned about the potential for additional or shifted documentation elements creating an extra burden to current nursing workflows. Our overarching comments are the following:
1.We recommend an evaluation of the ePrior Authorization pilot implementations from a clinical workflow perspective with full transparency of the results.
2.We encourage the inclusion of nursing stakeholders in ePrior Authorization implementations.
3.Where possible, we urge CMS to simplify and/or eliminate prior authorization processes.
Additionally, ANI would like to offer following specific comments regarding the proposed requirements:
•We support and advocate for app developers to follow industry best practices, including the CARIN Alliance's Code of Conduct and the ONC Model Privacy Notice (MPN) as described.

•We are in favor of the adoption of USCDI data classes for aspects of clinical information such as Immunizations, Procedures, and Assessment and Plan of Treatment, that support e-prior authorization. Accommodating the demographic characteristics contributing to health disparities (e.g., language, health/digital literacy) will help to ensure equity requirements and standardization of data for the PARDD API.

•Using deep learning AI methods for submitted clinical data could be used to inform the review and e-prior authorization approval process and expedite a ‘simulated consensus expert human judgment’ decision. To ensure transparency, medical accuracy and lack of bias, AI algorithms should be subject to public review with certification against clinical cases.

•We applaud CMS efforts to reduce the burden on providers for submitting prior authorization of required clinical data using FHIR standards and recognize automation of transactions could also be achieved with FHIR standards and CDS Hooks. An initial trigger from the Provider’s EHR to the payer’s system could deliver rules for approval following standardized query representation using CQL or other questionnaire

Payers should share data. Computable FHIR API help innovation and technical clarity. Payer-to-Provider FHIR APIs are central to real-time care coordination. Today pop health is often based on stale data abstraction. With Payer-to-Provider APIs providers can know the care their patient has gotten. “Opt out” is important because many patients can’t provide consent.

Payer-to-Payer and Payer-to-Provider APIs should use HL7 Bulk FHIR.

Providing PA decisions including denial reasons helps reduce repetitive PA. Please add meds. FHIR accelerators can build standards for PA decision documentation. Automation of PA is complicated. Clinical conditions addressed by prior authorization can be complex. Much non-standardized clinical information may have to be examined. The question for each piece of PARDD is what should be captured and shared. Coverage requirements discovery requires knowledge of the service to be covered and can be done with current payment codes. CRD API requirements could be 2026. Documentation Templates and Rules should use SMART on FHIR. Knowledge representation for thousands of disease / treatment combinations will be hard. CMS should require that PA decisions be based on publicly available CDS rather than private IP requiring licensing. Prior Authorization Support can subsume the current X12 278 standard and be done independent of X12. RESTful FHIR allows use of simple directory services and avoids clearinghouse overhead.

Re the RFI on MIPs incentives for TEFCA we suggest not going backwards technically. TEFCA uses an architecture from the 1990s before apps, REST, JSON and FHIR. We need deep computable interoperability not static medical document transfer.

The rule frames a choice between modern API interoperability and older document share. IHE on which TEFCA relies reflects a 1990s page-retrieval Internet. Computing TEFCA data requires complex negotiation with a QHIN and document parsing. There is not field level data access. By comparison, today with field level data, the Internet can support massive computing including entire app systems. Most phone apps use RESTful protocols and JSON streams of FHIR APIs. TEFCAs IHE architecture has no ability to generate population queries for provider performance or pandemic surveillance as the document is for one patient – TEFCA cannot query every document for every patient.

With the TEFCA RFI, CMS appears to be pondering directly opposite interoperability approaches. There are limited dollars for interoperability work and supporting conflicting approaches will offset the work the HL7 community has done.

Healthcare is moving from CCDA to its FHIR replacement. Individually retrievable data allows for efficiency whether for CDS, quality scores, fraud detection, patient empowerment, SDOH or any activity where computing algorithms help. Interoperability is a combo of transmission protocols and the form of the data. There has been discussion of “converting” TEFCA to use FHIR but FHIR as a payload in TEFCA won’t address the IHE transmission protocol lack of granular access. Rework of TEFCA for FHIR would require major bespoke healthcare only programming in each EMR.

TEFCA QHINs require new APIs both for sending and getting patient record requests. Simpler to go directly to FHIR APIs as in the payer sections of the rule rather than build out a duplicative structure and then try to rebuild in a few years using FHIR. CMS should hold off on TEFCA incentives that will require full software rebuilds until TEFCA has shown it can effectively use FHIR.

CMSs NDH can provide these electronic endpoints at lower cost whether for FHIR APIs or document fetches.

CMS should consider workforce. TEFCA requires arcane healthcare-only coding and few have these obsolete skills.

We urge CMS to analyze whether networks designed to link incumbent EHRs while effectively discouraging new competitors by mandated use of brokers optimizes policy. TEFCAs closed nature is apparent in the failure of the involved parties to use globally accepted standards organizations and instead maintain control by operators historically affiliated with legacy EMR vendors.

Unambiguous support for the FHIR APIs in the first section of the rule should be the focus of interoperability.

comment:
I am writing in support of CMS’ proposals to improve interoperability and streamline electronic prior authorization. The agency’s proposal will help to relieve the immense burden prior authorization has placed on me and other providers. It is critical that CMS finalize the proposed rule to mitigate the unwarranted burden prior authorization has been on both patients and providers. I also encourage CMS to do more to address this issue. This rule is a step in the right direction, but additional major reforms need to be made to correct the problem of insurance companies putting profit above patients.

While I support CMS’ efforts overall, I urge the agency to see how arbitrary denials have a direct impact on the quality and overall benefits of essential medical services provided by physical therapists. PTs and other providers are continually experiencing more demanding, complicated, and burdensome utilization reduction polices. Often, my patients must postpone care due to seemingly arbitrary denials, which are overturned on appeal but at considerable time and expense to the provider; delays in making a determination; piecemeal approvals requiring the provider to repeatedly resubmit the same requests; and payment denials for lack of authorization even when it was properly obtained.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly patients and providers must be able to appeal any modification the payer makes to the request if they feel it was made in error.

I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, & the patient’s prior authorization decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. Additionally, a study from HHS’ Office of the Inspector General found that capitated payment models such as those under MA can encourage MAOs to deny prior authorization claims, including claims that would otherwise not be denied under traditional Medicare. My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care.

comment:
I strongly support the Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes Proposed Rule CMS-0057-P (“Rule”). My support is based upon my personal experience as a patient as well as my professional experience working in three of the USA’s largest hospital systems in roles ranging from staff to management. The Rule constitutes a positive step toward supporting patients and restraining the out of control financially exploitative and abusive bureaucratic practices that are central to the business models of health insurers and the healthcare industry.

From the cms.gov Rule Fact Sheet (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/advancing-interoperability-and-improving-prior-authorization-processes-proposed-rule-cms-0057-p-fact):
“While prior authorization has a role in health care, in that it can ensure that covered items and services are medically necessary and covered by the payer, patients, providers, and payers alike have experienced burden from the process.”
A personal case in point: My in-network physician has issued an order for me to undergo a preventive colorectal cancer screening procedure that the United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends for patients my age and has given the screening procedure the highest rating of Grade A. The screening procedure is subject to the no cost sharing provisions of Section 2713 of the Public Health Service Act.
My physician harbors no doubts about the efficacy of my undergoing the screening and thus, there is no doubt about the screening’s medical necessity. My insurer however, insists on the screening being subject to prior authorization (“PA”). This is just one example of payers using PA as an obstacle of complication and bureaucracy to impede and dissuade patients from receiving medically necessary care ordered by their physician. The excessive use of PAs by healthcare payers has become the equivalent of a strategic lawsuit against public participation, or “SLAPP” suits, by monied corporations.

From the cms.gov Rule Fact Sheet (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/advancing-interoperability-and-improving-prior-authorization-processes-proposed-rule-cms-0057-p-fact):
“Denial Reason: We are proposing to require impacted payers to include a specific reason when they deny a prior authorization request, regardless of the method used to send the prior authorization decision, to both facilitate better communication and understanding between the provider and payer and, if necessary, a successful resubmission of the prior authorization request.”
From a regulatory standpoint, NOT requiring payers to provide a specific reason for denying a prior authorization request is a failure of our government and a giveaway to the healthcare industry writ large. This part of the proposed Rule should already be in effect and I fully support its implementation.

From the cms.gov Rule Fact Sheet (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/advancing-interoperability-and-improving-prior-authorization-processes-proposed-rule-cms-0057-p-fact):
“Prior Authorization Time Frames: We are proposing to require impacted payers (not including QHP issuers on the FFEs) to send prior authorization decisions within 72 hours for expedited (i.e., urgent) requests and seven calendar days for standard (i.e., non-urgent) requests. We are, however, also seeking comment on alternative time frames with shorter turnaround times, for example, 48 hours for expedited requests and five calendar days for standard requests.”
A timeframe of 48 hours (for expedited requests) and 5 days for standard requests provides more than sufficient time for payers to make their decision. Given that payers have already proven themselves fully capable of running other parts of their business in a timely manner (e.g., collecting premiums, executing collection actions against patients), they certainly have the means and ability to meet a quite reasonable 48 hour timeframe and a 5 day timeframe as outlined above. This part of the proposed Rule should already be in effect and I fully support its implementation.

From the cms.gov Rule Fact Sheet (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/advancing-interoperability-and-improving-prior-authorization-processes-proposed-rule-cms-0057-p-fact):
“Prior Authorization Metrics: We are proposing to require impacted payers to publicly report certain prior authorization metrics by posting them directly on the payer’s website or via publicly accessible hyperlink(s) on an annual basis.”
Transparency is central to a better functioning healthcare sector of our economy. It empowers patients, helps to hold payers and providers accountable, and is assistive in identifying fraud, waste, and abuse within the healthcare industry. As U.S. Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis said: Sunlight is the best disinfectant. This part of the proposed Rule should already be in effect and I fully support its implementation.

comment:
On behalf of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), a non-profit professional organization of more than 67,000 primary care pediatricians, pediatric medical subspecialists, and pediatric surgical specialists dedicated to the health, safety and well-being of infants, children, adolescents, and young adults, I write in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) related to advancing interoperability and improving prior authorization (PA) processes.

While the Academy generally supports CMS efforts to reduce burden and streamline processes for patients and providers, we reiterate previous concerns that these efforts will have minimal impact if not universally accepted and followed by all payers. Clinicians cannot document differently for patients based on different insurers. Frequently, a physician believes a patient is covered by one payer but finds out another was responsible after the claim is denied. Due to the administrative burden, it is impossible for the physician to go back and change the way they documented the note. Unless there is a stipulation that mandates all payers follow CMS documentation requirements, this will not provide documentation relief to clinicians and – to the contrary – may add a burden. For these reasons, the AAP urges CMS to leverage a regulatory pathway that will apply to all health plans when mandating PA-related implementation guides and transaction standards in any future rulemaking.

Our specific comments and recommendations are attached.

comment:
Regarding Improving Prior Authorization Processes:

I am in support of having impacted payers send prior authorization decisions within seven calendar days for a standard (i.e., non-urgent requests). Many plans are taking 14 days in non-urgent cases. For certain surgical specialties, the goal is to get the procedure done as soon as possible. Allowing 2 weeks for prior auths seems longer than it should be.

Additionally, Surgeons generally work in blocked OR schedules. If one patient needs to have a procedure cancelled as their surgery date approaches, it can be difficult for the surgeon to move another patient up due to the prior auth time frames. This becomes frustrating to the surgeon who wants to use his entire block of time, and also to the hospital who wants all blocks filled as surgical volume helps to balance out medical volume financially for many hospitals.

comment: This rule is a start but is by no means sufficient to address the rampant abuse of Prior Authorization by insurance companies in the US today. We need major reform or complete elimination of this dangerous practice for ALL insurance companies. It's dangerous because these delays damage health. I was recently denied a Prior Auth by BCBS because a slight increase in dosing wasn't on the FDA label even though this is a common practice supported by clinical studies and peer-reviewed journals. I spoke with 3 different people at BCBS/CVS Caremark and none would provide me the reason for denial (which I had to hear about from my doctor) nor would they tell me how I could immediately address it. comment:
Alexandra Mugge
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Department of Health and Human Services
Attention: CMS-0057-P,
P.O. Box 8016 Baltimore, MD 21244-8016
Submitted electronically at http://www.regulations.gov

Re: Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes (CMS-0057-P)

Dear Administrator Mugge:

In the past few years, I have become increasingly frustrated with the prior authorization process for medications that I take. It used to be that I only needed a prior authorization for hospital procedures or stays. Now, however, at least 6 of the medications I take that have been prescribed by my doctor are requiring prior authorization. Not only is this a heavy burden on me as a patient, but it also puts an even heavier burden on my doctors’ offices.

I found out recently that the form that my doctor has to fill out to complete the prior authorization has at least 11 questions and requires a signature. Even when I have them send the information, the authorization is still denied and/or needs more information from the doctor.

In one case, when I finally was able to get the medicine in the last dosage I had, it had been 2 months since I had taken it because of prior authorization issues as well as supply chain issues. Since I didn’t have access to the medication for an extended period, the side-effects were extreme, painful and made me miss work. In order to start on a lower dose and ramp up the dosage again gradually, I needed to repeat the prior authorization process again which took even longer.

In another case, the drug my insurance company said I had to try first before they would authorize the medication my doctor wanted me to take, also needed a prior authorization. And the co-pay was even more than the original drug.

Streamlining prior authorization will help me as a patient follow the guidelines of my doctors better, put less stress on me and my health and prevent more costly medications and procedures in the future. In addition, regulating how insurance companies process prior authorizations will improve clarity of treatment plans and decrease the burden on all the staff at the offices with ongoing re-evaluations, documentation and follow up on waiting for approval or denial.

Thank you for your work and time!

Elizabeth Saneholtz

comment:
I am writing in support of CMS’ proposals to improve interoperability and streamline electronic prior authorization. I am a licensed physical therapist that has worked for 2 non -profit pediatric hospitals, working inpatient and outpatient services. During these 7 years, timely authorization has been the biggest factor for delay in care as the majority of our patient population we treat have Medicaid for their insurance coverage. This has led to many parents and patients who have been frustrated with how late services start. These patients are dealing with pain either post surgically or from injuries that have significant repercussions in how quickly they recover. I have also had patients who have been on a waiting list waiting for care and each week that goes by further delays their overall wellbeing, gross motor delays, and even additional procedures such as helmet use for structural head defects ( I.e Brachiocephaly, or plagiocephaly) due to parents having fears of which position is safe for the family or how to complete stretches safely to their infant.

Earlier this year, I had a patient who was post-surgical and waited for 18 business days (due to parent scheduling and waitlist) to be seen at the initial physical therapy evaluation. This patient had a fear of taking off the knee brace post-surgery and was an in a significant amount of pain with movement, and so when removed during our initial session patient had 3 pressure ulcers in the posterior aspect of his leg in each site where there was straps to tighten the brace. From the initial evaluation, It took 6 business days for our personnel to send the evaluation report to the surgeon who referred patient for signature (which is a requirement given by some insurances in order to receive authorization), It took 8 business days for the surgeon to sign the POC, 2 business days later our personnel submitted for authorization and received authorization 3 business days later. From the physical therapy evaluation until the approval from insurance, the patient had to wait (19 business days) a total over three weeks, the outcome could have been different if he had a different insurance that does not require authorization and starting care immediately after the evaluation is completed. Unfortunately, cases like this happen frequently and patient`s usually have to wait even longer as post-operative surgical patient’s get priority due to the complexity of their case and the significant importance of guiding the surgical healing to avoid adverse effects and to reduce overall pain level.

In a time where the CDC is actively attempting to combat the opioid overdose epidemic, physical therapy can play a crucial part in reducing the use of opioids. As physical therapy practitioner’s, we can provide patients with effective evidenced based care for pain management without a prescription and help these patient`s to manage, and alleviate their symptoms. However, in order to best do this timely care is of utmost importance, as drug dependence can occur with increased use, especially post operatively. The common diagnosis in which opioid drugs are being prescribed for according to the CDC include post-operative patients, pain due to musculoskeletal injuries, arthritis. All the common diagnosis in which physical therapist treat successfully on a daily basis, and is backed by numerous evidenced based research. Physical therapist attain a doctorate level education to be able to help patients by providing evidence based care for pain management, alleviation of pain, and ultimately return to a more active lifestyle to improve the patient`s overall quality of life.

In closing, thank you for your consideration to this very important rule that would improve the process of authorization. I am in full support of streamlining the authorization process including providing comprehensive denial information to assure that therapist and appropriate personnel can correct the error in a quick manner. The current authorization process not only affects patient care and outcome, but is leading to therapist burnout and increasing administrative burden.

comment:
On behalf of its membership, the Pharmacy Health Information Technology Collaborative (PHIT) is pleased to submit comments for CMS-0057-P: Medicare Program, et al. Pharmacists provide essential, patient-centered care services to their patients, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries. Pharmacists use health IT, provider directories, telehealth, e-prescribing (eRx), electronic medical record (EMR)/electronic health record (EHR) systems, and certified EHR technology (CEHRT) to help manage patients’ health needs. PHIT supports the use of these systems, which are important to pharmacists in working with other health care providers to provide longitudinal person-centered care planning, needed medications, and transmit patient information related to overall patient care, transitions of care, immunization, medication lists, medication allergies, allergy reactions, patient problem lists, smoking status, and social determinants of health (SDOH). Pharmacists also use health IT for reporting to public health agencies (e.g., immunization reporting), clinical decision support services/knowledge artifacts, drug formulary checking, and comprehensive medication management (CMM). Attached are PHIT comments pertaining to the improving prior authorization processes portion of the proposed rule. PHIT agrees that there is a separate process for prior authorization for drugs and understands why CMS decided not to cover drugs in this proposed rule nor apply the Prior Authorization Requirements, Documentation, and Decision (PARDD) Application Programming Interface (API) to drugs at this time.
Although the proposal excludes drugs, it must be noted that payers will still need to communicate with pharmacists or providers may want to work pharmacists under collaborative practice agreements. This is because pharmacists, who are health care providers, provide medication therapy management (MTM) services and other clinical services to patients. In some instances, pharmacists submit services that require prior authorization to payers and use the health care claim and payment information standard X12 837 for payment. As discussed by CMS, the prior authorization request for these services may be submitted using the adopted HIPAA X12 278 standard for medical items and services, which include clinical services.

comment:
I am writing in support of CMS’ proposals to improve interoperability and streamline electronic prior authorization. The agency’s proposal will help to relieve the immense burden prior authorization has placed on me and other providers. It is critical that CMS finalize the proposed rule to mitigate the unwarranted burden prior authorization has been on both patients and providers. I also encourage CMS to do more to address this issue. This rule is a step in the right direction, but additional major reforms need to be made to correct the problem of insurance companies putting profit above patients.

While I support CMS’ efforts overall, I urge the agency to see how arbitrary denials have a direct impact on the quality and overall benefits of essential medical services provided by physical therapists. PTs and other providers are continually experiencing more demanding, complicated, and burdensome utilization reduction polices. Often, my patients must postpone care due to seemingly arbitrary denials, which are overturned on appeal but at considerable time and expense to the provider; delays in making a determination; piecemeal approvals requiring the provider to repeatedly resubmit the same requests; and payment denials for lack of authorization even when it was properly obtained.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly patients and providers must be able to appeal any modification the payer makes to the request if they feel it was made in error.

I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, and the patient’s prior authorization decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. Additionally, a study from HHS’ Office of the Inspector General found that capitated payment models such as those under MA can encourage MAOs to deny prior authorization claims, including claims that would otherwise not be denied under traditional Medicare. My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care

comment:
As a nation, whether healthcare is a national public program or privatized, the United States stands to only benefit if the healthcare system is improved on and more streamlined. Efficiency would look like better quality care with short wait times for patients and incentivized providers to offer that quality care patients want. Efficiency would also look like one interoperable system with healthcare data accessible by patients and necessary providers so data is thorough, complete and reliable. Systems in places such as prescription drug monitoring programs would work more efficiently. Mental healthcare would be more streamlined and patients can get the help they need quickly and efficiently. Entities such as the Veterans Affairs can have better information on their at-risk veterans if systems were interoperable.
I believe this proposed rule is essential to improve patient experience within the health care system. While complete interoperability in the current United States health market is yet to be a reality, I believe other healthcare system models have shown that a universal electronic health records system is overall beneficial for patients and providers. We see examples such as the Republic of Korea (South Korea). South Korea has a single national healthcare system and digitizing medical records into a single system has been shown to be a lot easier to implement. The benefits are not just autonomy of one’s health and medical records, but it serves a higher purpose when health institutions need to collect reliable data on disease control and prevention. It was shown that even for the COVID-19 pandemic, contact tracing was significantly more effective within a single digitalized system.
I believe this proposed rule is a great step in the right direction especially for healthcare services and programs that are federally funded. Not only will it allow clearer healthcare data, but it would simplify prior authorization processes for patients and providers alike. One of the challenges we see within Medicare and Medicaid systems is the long-winded and often confusing process to receive prior authorization. Streamlining this process will allow for quicker and better-quality care for patients and less time spent navigating these processes as a provider. I think it would be especially beneficial for patients who might have certain barriers that may make it especially difficult to navigate their health and multiple providers within their Medicare program or other federal program. Patients no longer would have to go through providers to access necessary paperwork or health data and providers can spend more time treating patients instead of fulfilling document requests.
However, there does pose a risk in systems such as a single electronic medical record. These systems are made to hold large amounts of personal information. There are concerns of data breaches. Therefore, systems need to be put in place to ensure that personal information is encrypted or safe. So far cohorts such as South Korea have shown that autonomy over one’s health data has enhanced public health. Another concern I have with the proposed regulation is how it might affect individuals in rural areas or lesser developed regions of the nation who are still utilizing federal health services. How can using interoperable electronic health record systems be enforced in areas where oversight might not be as keen? Do private practices that see patients in Medicare or other federal program incur those costs to transition to these electronic health records? While the proposal is positive and moving in the direction the nation needs, there are concerns of it’s feasibility as our nation does not have a single national system. My concerns are that it would take a lot of time, cooperative effort, and money to execute.

Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:

I am a physical therapist in private practice who has 16 years of experience providing therapy services to Medicare patients. I specialize in outpatient orthopedics. For these patients, delays in care or denial of medically necessary services means poorer outcomes. For providers like me, avoidable administrative burden means that instead of providing care to patients, I am spending time and resources on inefficient paperwork.

I want to thank CMS for its proposal to streamline administrative burden by establishing an automated prior authorization process. Reducing the number of times and how long it will take to process authorization requests is a welcome change. The proposed changes will address avoidable delays in patient care, achieve better health outcomes, and improve the care experience across providers, patients, and caregivers by significantly reducing wait times and increasing transparency around decisions.

In my experience, delays in care means that patients either don’t achieve optimal outcomes or it takes more visits overall; either of those options ends up costing the system more money. Last year I had to wait an average of 14 days before I got authorization to proceed for my patients covered by MA plans. Also, some of the time I got an approval only after resubmitting a request that was previously denied. The changes you are proposing will make a big difference to both my ability to provide timely patient care and save both time and money.

Thank you for taking my perspective into consideration as you craft regulations which could make a big impact on how readily my patients can access care—which will also impact how quickly I can help restore their function and reduce their pain.

Thank you,

comment:
Since 2013 when HITEKS Solutions Inc. started developing Epic integrated clinical applications within workflow, I realized that the stumbling block to Prior Authorizations was physicians and their ability to proactively justify procedures, medications and other care within their workflow.

The forms required by payers are really just another type of clinical note, which should have purview by the Clinical Documentation Improvement function of health care providers. An insurance form to justify Prior Authorization is no different from an H&P, progress note, or Discharge Note. It requires defining interoperability standards for the Prior Authorization forms not only at the level of the document, but also the specific clinical questions and their responses which are asked such as "What was the patient's outcome with an alternate previously taken medication?" and "What are the patient's specific diagnosis and co-morbidities that justify this medication or procedure?"

Answers to these questions require responses which include: Yes/No, Sentences to explain, Reference to existing parts of the digital medical chart such as an imaging study or pathology report, and so on. Each of these answer types requires a standard model with which a computer can understand it and deliver both the question and the responses in automated methods. The EHR vendor is not solely responsible to implement these interoperability standards because other analytics and CDI vendors have purview around the content of documentation in the chart which needs to be parsed and analyzed to return meaningful suggestions to the clinician to semi-automate their PA responses and then sign off on their for submission.

Physician documentation for these clinical justification questions must be signed off and made part of the legal medical record. Now there's an opportunity for CDI Functions and Physicians to shape these requirements.

Thank you for your time and attention.

Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:

I am writing to represent our company, a private practice physical therapy clinic that has been in business for over 17 years providing therapy services to Medicare patients. Our clinic specializes in outpatient orthopedic physical therapy and serves a large Medicare population base. For these patients, delays in care or denial of medically necessary services means poorer outcomes. For providers like ours, avoidable administrative burden means that instead of providing care to patients, our therapists spend needless time and resources on inefficient paperwork.

I want to thank CMS for its proposal to streamline administrative burden by establishing an automated prior authorization process. Reducing the number of times and how long it will take to process authorization requests is a welcome change. The proposed changes will address avoidable delays in patient care, achieve better health outcomes, and improve the care experience across providers, patients, and caregivers by significantly reducing wait times and increasing transparency around decisions.

In our experience, delays in care means that patients either don’t achieve optimal outcomes or it takes more visits overall; either of those options ends up costing the system more money. Last year we had to wait many days before receiving authorization to proceed with patients covered by MA plans. Also, many times we finally got an approval only after resubmitting a request that was previously denied. The changes you are proposing will make a big difference to both our ability to provide timely patient care and save both time and money.

Thank you for taking our perspective into consideration as you craft regulations which could make a big impact on how readily our patients can access care—which will also impact how quickly we can help restore their function and reduce their pain.

Thank you,

Jay Mehta

Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:

I am a physical therapist in private practice who has 12 years of experience providing therapy services to Medicare patients. I specialize in orthopedic physical therapy. For these patients, delays in care or denial of medically necessary services means poorer outcomes. For providers like me, avoidable administrative burden means that instead of providing care to patients, I am spending time and resources on inefficient paperwork.

I want to thank CMS for its proposal to streamline administrative burden by establishing an automated prior authorization process. Reducing the number of times and how long it will take to process authorization requests is a welcome change. The proposed changes will address avoidable delays in patient care, achieve better health outcomes, and improve the care experience across providers, patients, and caregivers by significantly reducing wait times and increasing transparency around decisions.

Also, much of the time I got an approval only after resubmitting a request that was previously denied. The changes you are proposing will make a big difference to both my ability to provide timely patient care and save both time and money.

Thank you for taking my perspective into consideration as you craft regulations which could make a big impact on how readily my patients can access care—which will also impact how quickly I can help restore their function and reduce their pain.

Thank you,

comment:
Our organization has worked in tandem with our customers to facilitate a cohesive experience across all platforms for payors, providers, and member/patients, with the primary objective of keeping the patient at the center of care. While we recognize and appreciate many aspects of the proposed rule, we would like to provide comments on both areas of concern and solicited areas.
We strongly endorse our customers' management of turn-around-times and the authorization process, having witnessed a decrease in prior authorization requirements that has increased patient access, reduced administrative burden, and enhanced provider relationships. However, not all payers have achieved the same level of success in reducing requirements, and providers must serve patients across various payers, each with different authorization requirements. Thus, it is crucial to consider the percentage of procedures requiring prior authorization, with organizations that have already scaled back significantly having a shorter list to incorporate into their gold carding options. Furthermore, as payers introduce more gold carding features, a process for quality checking current gold card providers must be established to ensure they are still adhering to the required standards. While we agree that gold carding can alleviate provider burden, the downstream effect of payers conducting post-service reviews of claims and acquiring clinical documentation to ensure that gold card status is not being abused may increase operational requirements for payors. Therefore, we recommend that clarity regarding the revocation of gold carding is outlined in advance.
Additionally, because gold carding will increase the number of disallowed retrospective reviews, we suggest that as an alternative to cold carding, the regulation should encourage API-based EMR/UM system level integration so that the interaction burden on the provider is removed, and the result/determination is visible in the EMR.
Our organization and our customers are committed to promoting health equity, and we have carefully considered the request for comments on the impact of gold carding on health equity. At present, patient demographics are not taken into account for authorizations, with patient information limited to determining benefit coverage and eligibility, as well as turn-around-times. From our perspective, the socioeconomic availability of care would be minimally impacted by the gold card rule alone. While we recognize that there are several opportunities to improve health equity, part of the disparity stems from the utilization of the healthcare system, lack of access to a primary provider, and other factors. We do not believe that prior authorization is the root cause of inequities in the healthcare system.
The practice of public reporting of certain metrics is useful in promoting transparency in healthcare organizations. However, a mere display of the number of approvals or denials may be misleading in certain instances. In cases where an organization has reduced the number of procedures requiring prior authorizations, their overall authorization rate may appear lower than that of organizations reviewing a higher percentage of procedures.
Our customers have initiated several programs that enhance patient outcomes, and prior authorization can serve as a trigger for care management to assist in making informed decisions regarding treatment options, surgery preparation, education opportunities, and post-discharge options for care needs. Therefore, we should not focus solely on the number of approvals and denials, but also recognize the role that prior authorizations play in reducing unnecessary or avoidable procedures, and better preparing patients for post-discharge and more favorable outcomes.
With regard to reducing turn-around-times, we believe that distinguishing between urgent and non-urgent requests is of utmost importance. The regulation states that a provider can indicate the need for an urgent request when a standard timeframe could seriously jeopardize life, health, or ability to attain/maintain/regain maximum function. However, this designation has the potential to be abused or overused. Hence, we require checks and balances to ensure quality control on the use of urgent vs. standard requests. If during the prior authorization review process or post-service review, the procedure is deemed non-urgent, we recommend instituting restrictions or controls to prevent its misuse.
Our organization is committed to change and collaborates with our partners to enhance the overall provider, payer, patient experience. We are enthusiastic about continued innovation in the healthcare industry to better support the health care journey of patients, payers, and providers.

comment:
Prior Authorization, when appropriately performed, ensures that patients receive evidence-based care and improves rather than harms patient outcomes. Secondarily, this approach has been shown to reduce out of pocket expenses for the patients. Our understanding of what drives the development of metastatic disease and how to adequately treat newly diagnosed malignancies literally changes on a monthly basis. The idea that even the best trained oncologist is always up to date on therapies is not credible. A potential delay of a few days to ensure optimal care is actually in the patient’s best interest and not motivated by financial gain for the insurance industry or an attempt to weaken the doctor/patient relationship.

Tumor doubling time is quite variable but for breast cancer, a good model for all solid tumors, is estimated to vary from 45-260 days. Furthermore, from inception to clinical presentation, most tumors have doubled in size between 20 and 30 times. This translates into the tumor being present for at least several years prior to the initiation of any definitive treatment. Once a solid tumor, in contradistinction from blood-based malignancies like leukemia or lymphoma, has been diagnosed many additional diagnostic and therapeutic interventions are necessary before starting either surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation.

Most surgical societies recommend scheduling surgery within 90 days of a cancer diagnosis. Data indicates that chemotherapy can be delayed for up to 120 days for women with a newly diagnosed breast cancer. Even properly staging a patient, which is critical to developing an integrated and multi-modality approach to the disease, adds weeks to the interval between diagnosis and initiation of any form of treatment. For these reasons, ensuring appropriate review timeframes to make the best decision for the patient and avoiding failed therapy can be critical. Accelerated review timeframes increase the risk of failed or non-optimal therapies.

Truly knowledgeable physicians should explain to their patients how this short delay is actually in their best interest and will ensure the best possible outcome.

Often, my patients must postpone care due to seemingly arbitrary denials, which are overturned on appeal but at considerable time and expense to the provider; delays in making a determination; piecemeal approvals requiring the provider to repeatedly resubmit the same requests; and payment denials for lack of authorization even when it was properly obtained.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While I support CMS’ efforts overall, I urge the agency to see how arbitrary denials have a direct impact on the quality and overall benefits of essential medical services provided by physical therapists. PTs and other providers are continually experiencing more demanding, complicated, and burdensome utilization reduction polices. Often, my patients must postpone care due to seemingly arbitrary denials, which are overturned on appeal but at considerable time and expense to the provider; delays in making a determination; piecemeal approvals requiring the provider to repeatedly resubmit the same requests; and payment denials for lack of authorization even when it was properly obtained.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly patients and providers must be able to appeal any modification the payer makes to the request if they feel it was made in error.

I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, and the patient’s prior auth decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. Additionally, a study from HHS’ Office of the Inspector General found that capitated payment models such as those under MA can encourage MAOs to deny prior authorization claims, including claims that would otherwise not be denied under traditional Medicare. My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care.

comment:
RE: CMS-0057-P
I am the practice administrator for a small private practice physical therapy clinic. I perform 100% of all the billing, prior authorizations, claim denial disputes and other interactions with health plans. I have 8 years of experience in this area.

This proposed rule change intends to improve the process of securing prior authorization by promoting and standardizing various electronic methods (API's) for interacting with the various payer organizations such as Medicare Advantage and Medicaid entities. It also intends to reduce the burden on healthcare providers when obtaining the prior authorizations.

While I am, in general, highly in favor of reducing the ever increasing administrative burden on healthcare providers, it escapes me how this proposed rule change will actually accomplish this objective. With regards to prior authorization within the context of private practice Physical Therapy, I believe the first question is what value is actually provided by this process. I am not aware of any data supporting the usefulness or value of prior authorization and I have attempted to get this question addressed through several avenues with no answers provided. Is it simply assumed prior authorization for Physical Therapy is a positive cost/benefit? At present, traditional Medicare does not require prior authorization but many Medicare Advantage plans do require it. In my state of Oklahoma, all PT requires prior auth if Medicaid is primary. Of all the authorizations I have worked with, Medicaid is absolutely the worst. It can take weeks for status and may be rejected for trivial/non-medical issues forcing a restart of the entire process. We have seen patients discontinue or not even start PT due to this problem.

Other illogical issues with prior auth can include needing a magic crystal ball to answer specific treatment details before ever encountering the patient. Some auths require knowledge of exact numbers of each CPT code to be used, for example.

How much will it cost to implement these proposals across all platforms and what benefit will actually be provided? Instead of, apparently, mandating prior authorizations for all of these constituents under all conditions why not study and release data on the actual benefits of performing prior authorizations? Perhaps, in some situations, it makes sense. If so, specify those situations and remove all of the burden from those for whom there is no discernible net benefit.

My personal experience with prior authorization, outside of the state's Medicaid program, is it is always granted with no changes. I do not perceive any net benefit but the cost in time and nuisance is considerable. My suggestion, therefore, is to completely remove the need for prior authorization for private practice Physical Therapy.

comment: While in favor of the proposed changes to the Prior Auth turn around times, what is missing here, and is not discussed, is the prior authorization process for patients who are currently in the hospital and pending authorization to the next level of care so that the patient can discharge.  Leaving a patient in the hospital setting fo 14 days (or even up to 7 under the new proposal) is a huge burden on the hospital who needs the beds for patients who require IP care.  One could say to submit the authorization for post-acute care earlier - however, MA payors or other payors will not typically make a decision regarding medical necessity unless and until they see clinical information of how the patient is functioning at the time they are ready for that next level of care. So submitting early does not help as the payors cannot apparently think or plan ahead.  I would propose that Prior Authorization decisions for post-acute care for patients currently in the hospital be held to the same TAT requirements as Inpatient authorizations - or 24 hours.  Most managed care providers do not have the capability to find those prior auth or pre-sevice requests that are pending discharge among their vast volume of other pre-service requests so a provider must call the payor, hope to speak to someone knowledgeable, and hope they can find the request and are willing to expedite processing.  But even if submitted as an expedited request, post-acute/discharge requests really do not meet that specified definition AND 72 hours for a patient to sit in a hospital waiting to move to the next level of care is unacceptable - not only for that patient but for the patients in the ED waiting on a bed.  Please consider post-acutre care authorization for patients pending dischage in a category of its own and apply a more reasonable turn around time for those request akin to the IP authorization expectation.

I am a physical therapist in private practice who has 5 years of experience providing therapy services to Medicare patients. I specialize in Pelvic Floor and Orthopedic Physical Therapy. CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. comment:
While this may be a small step in the right direction, the delay in care is only a portion of the problem. Prior authorizations take patient care time away from physicians as well as medical staff--sometimes causing staff to be on hold with insurances for upwards of an hour. In order to help our practices stay afloat, physicians need to be able to bill for the time spent attending to a prior authorization requirement. Decreasing the turn around time for prior authorizations does not mitigate the need for a physician to spend extra time after a patient visit writing and alternative medication as dictated by the prior authorization. In the context of care for patients with cancer related pain, I have had opioids denied by insurance companies for patients in an acute cancer related pain crisis triggering patients to request Physician Aid in Dying. So, again, in a healthcare system that is losing physicians en mass, it is imperative that we use our physicians to see patients, not bog them down with administrative tasks. If there are to be administrative tasks, we need to be reimbursed for these costs.
Furthermore, most prior authorization requests are ultimately approved. This means that the time spent for prior authorizations really only creates a delay in care.
I would also argue that public prior authorization reporting should also include a reason for prior authorization denial, e.g. cost, medically not indicated, experimental treatment, or similar. This would allow us to track whether the prior authorizations are largely being administered to further quality of care or further financial savings.

While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:



I am a physical therapist aide in private practice. For patients under medicare delays in care or denial of medically necessary services means poorer outcomes. For providers like me, avoidable administrative burden means that instead of providing care to patients, I am spending time and resources on inefficient paperwork.



I want to thank CMS for its proposal to streamline administrative burden by establishing an automated prior authorization process. Reducing the number of times and how long it will take to process authorization requests is a welcome change. The proposed changes will address avoidable delays in patient care, achieve better health outcomes, and improve the care experience across providers, patients, and caregivers by significantly reducing wait times and increasing transparency around decisions.



In my experience, delays in care means that patients either don’t achieve optimal outcomes or it takes more visits overall; either of those options ends up costing the system more money. The changes you are proposing will make a big difference to both my ability to provide timely patient care and save both time and money.



Thank you for taking my perspective into consideration as you craft regulations which could make a big impact on how readily my patients can access care—which will also impact how quickly I can help restore their function and reduce their pain.



Thank you,

On behalf of the Vermont Agency of Human Services and Department of Vermont Health
Access, our state Medicaid agency, I wish to offer the following additional comments on the proposed rule, Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization [CMS-0057-P]:

with potential app users.

comment:
Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:

I am a physical therapist in private practice who has over 2 years of experience providing therapy services to Medicare patients. I specialize in outpatient orthopedics which as you know is a common practice location for patients who have Medicare. For these patients, delays in care or denial of medically necessary services means poorer outcomes. For providers like me, avoidable administrative burden means that instead of providing care to patients, I am spending time and resources on inefficient paperwork.

I want to thank CMS for its proposal to streamline administrative burden by establishing an automated prior authorization process. Reducing the number of times and how long it will take to process authorization requests is a welcome change. The proposed changes will address avoidable delays in patient care, achieve better health outcomes, and improve the care experience across providers, patients, and caregivers by significantly reducing wait times and increasing transparency around decisions.

In my experience, delays in care means that patients either don’t achieve optimal outcomes or it takes more visits overall; either of those options ends up costing the system more money. Last year I had to wait an average of 10 days before I got authorization to proceed for my patients covered by MA plans. Also, about 60 % of the time I got an approval only after resubmitting a request that was previously denied. The changes you are proposing will make a big difference to both my ability to provide timely patient care and save both time and money.

Thank you for taking my perspective into consideration as you craft regulations which could make a big impact on how readily my patients can access care—which will also impact how quickly I can help restore their function and reduce their pain.

Thank you,


Dr. Taylor Mogg, PT, DPT
NCEPT Physical Therapy
