comment:
3/13/2023

Dear Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services:

Thank you for the opportunity to respond to the Proposed Final Rule CMS-0057-P. The rule promises to streamline prior authorization processes and increase access to relevant patient data for healthcare providers. However, these improvements need to be built upon a robust foundation of APIs that were required by the 2020 Final Rule for Interoperability and Patient Access. It is important that CMS ensure that APIs required by the 2020 Rule fully address the use cases described in the Rule.

In particular, the Provider Directory API requirements are not yet universally implemented by all payers. Defacto Health has integrated payers’ Provider Directory APIs since the enforcement date in July 2021. While testing and integrating with payers’ Provider Directory APIs, we observed the following:

27% of payers have not yet published a Provider Directory API.
34% of payers’ Provider Directory APIs have issues blocking integration.
46% of these APIs lack key data to help patients determine whether a provider is in-network for a particular plan-product offered by the payer.
22% have non-compliant authentication requirements or registration errors.

Defacto Health recommends these requirements for Provider Directory APIs be adopted:
1. Require data in API that links Practitioners and Organizations to Insurance Plans.
2. Require that names of Insurance Plans are the same as those on members’ insurance cards, member handbooks, and those used as filters on payers’ web directories.
3. Contact information or support resolution methods are published in payer portals.
4. Information on APIs are documented on payers’ websites (and not their vendors’).
5. Enforce the requirement for publicly accessible Provider Directory APIs.

For the Prior Authorization use case, an important prerequisite is that members select in-network providers that participate in their health plan. Inaccurate or unavailable Plan-Insurance information can negatively impact Prior Authorization:

1. In cases where they have selected an out-of-network provider, the patient may be responsible for completing Prior Authorization with the payer.
2. Even if the payer approves a Prior Authorization, because the patient has selected an out-of-network provider, she may be responsible for higher out-of-pocket expenses. 3. If an in-network provider must refer a patient to another in-network provider for an Prior Authorization-approved service, then it is important that in-network providers are readily searchable by the referring provider.

These hurdles can be overcome with accurate “Insurances Accepted” information in Provider Directory APIs. To ensure that the future state of Prior Authorization is streamlined, it is therefore important that payers implement functional Provider Directory and Patient Access APIs required by the 2020 Final Rule.

Finally, regulatory enforcement of current Final Rule requirements (i.e., Patient Access API, Provider Directory API) sets a precedence for payers on Proposed Final Rule requirements. Lack of enforcement of current Rule requirements may put at risk the implementation of Proposed Final Rule requirements.

We look forward to future collaboration on interoperability and patient access.

Sincerely,

Ron Urwongse, Co-Founder, Defacto Health
T.J. Theogaraj, Co-Founder, Defacto Health

Attention: CMS-0057-P

Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges, Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Eligible Clinicians, and Eligible Hospitals and Critical Access Hospitals in the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program

MMM Healthcare (MMM) appreciates this opportunity to comment on the Proposed Rule CMS-0057-P, below are our comments and recommendations regarding this Rule:

We would like to clarify if CMS intention is to only include contracted Providers who have both a contractual relationship with the payer and a treatment relationship with the patient. Can CMS further define "treatment relationship with the patient"?

Also, can CMS further define Healthcare facility, and which facilities are considered, only contracted or out of network?

The Proposal also requires that impacted payers make available any of the applicable patient data with a date of service on or after January 1, 2016; is CMS intention to include all data since 2016 and not only the last 5 years as previously proposed?

Related to the opt in/out policy, will any type of consent qualify as an Opt In? Is there any required language that must be included? Can this opt-in be included in the HIPAA PHI authorization form or any other enrollment material?

CMS mentioned is withdrawing the December 2020 CMS Interoperability proposed rule and issuing this new proposed rule. What about the enforcement of CMS-9115-F?

Lastly, the reduction in timeframes will provide additional burden to Plans and CMS should consider maintaining current decision timeframes until all these programs are implemented and working as intended. Plans are heavily audited regarding these timeframes and without final requirements, is impossible to measure if these reduction in timeframes are even feasible.

We value the partnership that we have developed with CMS and welcome the opportunity to discuss our recommendations. Should you have any questions or wish to discuss our comments further, please contact us.

Sincerely,

While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly patients and providers must be able to appeal any modification the payer makes to the request if they feel it was made in error.

I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, and the patient’s prior authorization decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. comment:
Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:

Premier Inc. appreciates the opportunity to submit comments to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) regarding its Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to advance interoperability and improve prior authorization processes across CMS-regulated health programs. The proposed rule seeks public comment on CMS’ proposals to ensure timely access to care and improve data sharing among Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and issuers of Qualified Health Plans (QHPs) on the federally-facilitated Exchanges.

Premier appreciates CMS’ commitment to improving access to care and enabling better data exchange among providers, patients and payers. Specifically, Premier recommends the following:

•Require payers to disclose via Patient Access application programming interfaces (APIs) the specific coverage criteria that were and were not satisfied for prior authorization requests that result in denials;
•Finalize proposed requirements for payers to build and maintain Provider Access APIs, while ensuring that patient data collected by vertically-integrated, payer-owned providers and health services companies is included in the available data;
•Require that data received by payers through the payer-to-payer data exchange be shared on the Provider Access API so that providers have access to longitudinal data on patients’ healthcare and can provide the most appropriate care;
•Finalize proposed requirements for affected payers to build and maintain Prior Authorization Requirements, Documentation, and Decision (PARDD) APIs, creating a single electronic point of entry for the payer’s prior authorization processes that holds potential for integrating into the provider workflow;
•No later than 12 months following the publication of a final rule, require affected payers to deliver prior authorization responses within 72 calendar hours for standard, non-urgent services and within 24 calendar hours for urgent services; and
•In the longer term, develop programs to provide affected payers with additional flexibilities and/or financial rewards for implementing real-time prior authorization programs with contracted providers.

Premier welcomes the opportunity to provide feedback on the proposals included in this NPRM. Our detailed recommendations are included in the attachment.

I am a medical practice manager but have also been the victim of delayed or expensive care due to the need for prior auth. On two separate occasions I have had surgery and when I went to pick up my post op pain medicine however upon arrival the pharmacy told me that it needed prior authorization. becuase I work in healthcare I knew the game and that I could op to pay cash for the whole RX amount or take 5 day supply and then have my doctor send in a new prescription for the remaining amount. It cost me almost $100 for something that is covered by my $10 RX Copay. Again I chose that option because I know the game but patients that are not in healthcare with that knowledge have to go through so much hassle. It actually results in a lot of time and labor of a lot of staff too. It endes up with a lot of unnecessary calls back and forth between the office, patient and pharmacy with most of the frustration directed at medical office staff/provider and in most cases accusatory in nature that we did not do our part.

Regarding other services like MRI's needing authorization or being denied due to lack of medical necessity the providers clinical knowledge is completely removed from the process. It is almost like some customer service rep with the insurance company is just using a checklist and not even taking the providers clinical exam in to consideration. In our specialty we provider conservative treatments to alleviate pain and prevent or prolong the need for surgery. In sme cases our providers can use ultrasound guidance for inject medication in to a joint but when it comes to the spinal column for something like a herniated disk and MRI prior confirms the physical exam findings but also give the provider valuable pathology to see the exact nature of pain, degree of disc herniation and nerve damage and in some cases stops up from doing an unnecessary conservative injection when the patient actually does need surgery.

March 12, 2023

The Honorable Chiquita Brooks-LaSure Administrator
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
Department of Health and Human Services
7500 Security Boulevard
Baltimore, MD 21244-1850

Submitted electronically to regulations.gov
Re: [CMS-0057-P] Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges, Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Eligible Clinicians, and Eligible Hospitals and Critical Access Hospitals in the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program

Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure,

The North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society (NANOS), which represents over 680 ophthalmologists and neurologists, appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule regarding requirements on Medicare and Medicaid programs to improve and streamline the electronic exchange of healthcare data, particularly in terms of addressing Medicare Advantage (MA) electronic prior authorization (e-PA) requirements.

NANOS would like to thank CMS for taking major steps in modernizing how the American healthcare system and healthcare plans cooperate and collaborate to ensure optimal outcomes for patients and their quality of life. By directly addressing the current issues in MA PA processes and supporting the use of interoperability processes to streamline communication, we believe the provisions of this rule will reduce administrative burden for providers and prevent delayed patient care due to inappropriate PA denials.

Members of Congress have highlighted their concerns about the use of PA by MA programs and the barriers to care these processes put in place for their constituents as well. In the 117th Congress, a bipartisan coalition of over half the Senate, three quarters of the House, and over 500 organizations from across all sectors (patients, providers, pharmaceutical industry, medical technology groups, etc.) rallied around the Improving Seniors’ Timely Access to Care Act (S. 3018/H.R. 3173). Last fall, the House passed the legislation on a unanimous voice vote. Unfortunately, the original Congressional Budget Office scoring caused a delay in the bill’s passage through the Senate, leaving this issue still unaddressed.
We appreciate CMS taking up the issue of electronic PA and are glad to see the many places where language in the legislation and this proposed rule align.

Both the proposed rule and legislation acknowledge that PA:
•Plays an important role in utilization management, but it can be misused or overused, creating
•considerable challenges for patients, providers, and payers;
•Presents a serious health risk for patients when care is delayed;
•Increases provider and payer burden due to inconsistent payer policies, provider workflow challenges, and unpredictable use of electronic standards; and
•Contributes to significant provider burnout.

The e-PA Proposed Rule and the legislation also include similar elements:
•Require MA plans to adopt e-PA;
•Ensure that MA plans respond to PA requests within specific timeframes;
•Require public reporting on the use of PA;
•Support waiver or modification of PA requirements based on provider performance; and
•Recognize that health plans’ proprietary interfaces and web portals through which providers submit their requests remain inefficient and burdensome.

NANOS strongly supports the regulatory changes set forth in this proposed rule that mirror the legislation and we urge the agency to swiftly finalize these policies in 2023 to ensure that all Medicare beneficiaries have equal access to covered benefits.
We appreciate the opportunity to provide the physician perspective on MA PA and looks forward to working closely with CMS to further refine regulatory requirements to protect access to sight-saving care. If you have any questions or need additional information, do not hesitate to contact us.

Sincerely,

Prem S. Subramanian, MD, PhD
North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society

comment:
As a Masters prepared Certified Nurse Case Manager for 20+ years at a Pediatric Rehabilitation Hospital and a Major East Coast University Medical center, the increasingly frequent, and broad ranging requests for insurance providers pre-authorization requirements, have gotten more complicated, with increasingly lengthy review times for approval. What was originally a simple form explaining why expensive testing or a procedure was required ( based on the patient’s prior medical records) and a 1-2 day turnaround, has become a complicated multi-page /multi-screen application, not only requiring a physician signature on a form with basic information compiled by Case Managers and Medical Records staff, but now a LENGTHY direct telephonic “Peer to Peer” confirmation phone call between the providing doctor and whichever MD the insurance company has hired to review the precert request, taking our Medical staff away from patient treatment time. That review is frequently done by a physician hired part time from the insurance who may have no specialty experience (ie: a Pediatrician reviewing for a complex Adult Cardiac test or procedure). Those reviews now take an inordinate amount of treating provider time to conduct, and sometimes 2-3 weeks turnaround time for an insurance determination. If that is a denial, the complex, multi-level insurance appeal process, can take weeks to months to complete. Meanwhile the patient has to decide to either delay the treatment OR agree to
Pay OUT OF POCKET (hundreds to thousands of dollars) to guarantee doing the needed procedure WITHOUT insurance company pre-authorization!

There certainly needs to be REASONABLE use of expensive tests and procedures, but one of the MAJOR reasons for the increase in demand for certified Nurse Care Managers, is to ensure that APPROPRIATE services are utilized.

The delays have adversely affected timely medical treatment given to patients. Shortening the turnaround time for an insurance pre certification decision will vastly improve patient care.

Re: Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes (CMS-0057-P)

I have been a PT for 27 years practicing and am a Board-Certified Specialist in Neurologic PT. I work in a large healthcare system in the outpatient neurologic setting and am the Program Director for our PT residency programs which include rotations in acute care and inpatient rehab. I also work in our wheelchair seating and mobility clinic. My patients have a wide variety of neurologic diagnoses including degenerative diseases such as Parkinson's Disease, Multiple Sclerosis, and ALS along with stroke, brain injury, and spinal cord injury.

CMS needs to streamline the process for prior authorization. Each entity should NOT be able to create their own rules and process and paperwork on how to obtain authorization for skilled services. We have one local managed Medicare plan that requires the therapist to fill out a separate standardized form and basically rewrite the PT evaluation into boxes and comments that don't even actually make sense for the patient case. Our evaluations are far more thorough, follow APTA guidelines on best practice, and follow Joint Commission guidelines. It is a waste of a therapist's time to then have to complete an additional form unique to each insurance company. The form then has to be printed, scanned, and faxed. When this happens there is often several weeks delay in authorization to begin treatment after an evaluation. Often in the interim the patient becomes deconditioned, falls, develops pressure sores, and contractures. Their long-term potential is limited due to delayed access to care due to the multilayered prior authorization process. This is the number one reason I would leave the field of PT and cause of burn out among PTs and other health care professionals. I implore you to decrease the administrative burden of prior authorization to improve access to care. Prevent insurance providers from each creating their own system and forms. Standard documentation includes all of the relevant pieces of information for the insurance company to make a determination of need. Some companies also only approve 3-5 visits at a time. That is absolutely ridiculous when trying to rehab someone with a spinal cord injury. They then have to be removed from the schedule to wait for more authorized visits, lose the spot on the schedule, and have 2-3 weeks of time between sessions. which limits functional progress and is not best use of insurance dollars.

There needs to be more transparency in the process for prior authorization. The insurance companies develop their own hoops for practitioners to jump through that limit and delay patient access to care. There should also be requirements on the insurance company to respond to request within 24 hours. This is access to medical care and needs to be timely!

Insurers need to provide comprehensive detailed information on denials. I had a wheelchair denied for a person who had a spinal cord injury stating that evaluation needed to be done by a licensed PT. Literarily, the attached note had my PT evaluation attached, signed by me ( I am a licensed PT with 3 specialty certifications 2 of which are in wheelchair seating and mobility). I had to highlight that and fax it back to them. How absurd is that! The patient ended up waiting an extra 6 weeks to have access to the proper equipment. If we don't fully understand why something is denied a number of things occur; we may continue to submit for things that the insurance company won’t cover wasting everyone's time and resources, we can't learn the requirements for equipment and services to appropriately document and support our recommendations. Even our patients with high health literacy can't understand their own insurance plans. This creates a huge health care disparity for individuals from lower socioeconomical groups. The denials and details of the insurance plan should be written at the average reading level of an adult living in America. Having the details written in legal terms limits access to healthcare It should be clear what the policy states and requires for services to be covered. And can we stop having to have the doctor sign everything? I have 27 years of experience, I have a Doctor of Physical Therapy degree, and 3 specialty services. I spend 90 minutes with the patient, family , and a vendor and the insurance company will deny services if a medical doctor doesn't sign off. The MDs I work with value my education and experience and sign off however because they are in so many locations and have their own EMR sometimes it is sitting on their desk for a week and then waiting for office people to fax for another week. It needs to stop. Hard working, good, kind clinicians are leaving healthcare as they are so strapped in their ability to provide appropriate timely care due to paperwork and administrative burden.

From,

Jamie Dietrich, PT, DPT, NCS, ATP/SMS

comment:
16 February 2023

Chiquita Brooks-LaSure, Administrator
Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)

Re: CMS-2022-0190-0002, file code CMS-0057-P
Submitted to https://www.regulations.gov.

The Honorable Administrator Brooks-LaSure:

Thank you for opening a comment period on the proposed rule to reduce the clinical burden of prior authorization. The End Burnout Group is pleased to offer perspectives on the issue of prior authorization that may be seen as innovative or perhaps even radical.

The End Burnout Group (EBG) was founded by clinicians and health informatics professionals with the goal of eliminating the root causes of clinician burnout. Like CMS, EBG sees clinician burnout as a crisis. Immediate efforts, like streamlining prior authorization, are needed to reduce burdens now. EBG sees the current efforts to mitigate burden as critically necessary, but only the beginning of what is needed. If we do not ALSO work to eliminate root causes concurrent with these mitigation efforts, the burdens will continue to grow and at some point, mitigation will no longer be effective. At this time, EBG has identified 10 root causes of burnout. Prior authorization is one of those 10 causes. It is the view of EBG that prior authorization should be eliminated.

Burnout is a national crisis, and prior authorization (PA) is a contributor, as several references show in the proposed regulations document. PA has never demonstrated value and has only served to delay care. Indeed PA costs billions of dollars to practitioners, healthcare organizations, hospitals, patients and employers. Stanford professor Dr. Jeffrey Pfeffer showed in an article “Magnitude and Effects of “sludge” in benefits administration: How health insurance hassles burden workers and cost employers,” found at: https://jeffreypfeffer.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/AMD-Benefits-Pfeffer.pdf, the direct costs of administrative burden are approximately $21.57 Billion and PA is a major component. The estimated cost of work absence was another $26.4 Billion and the cost of lost productivity due to reduced satisfaction was approximately $95.6 Billion. These are real dollars lost, and likely not accounted for by other studies that look only at the cost and benefits to insurance companies for not covering needed treatments.

CMS should eliminate PA which will save billions of dollars, reduce care delays, and effectively and markedly reduce clinician burden. If eliminating PA is not the course that CMS wishes to take today, then the steps in these proposed regulations are worth taking now.

Please see the attached document for additional details.

Thank you for your consideration,

End Burnout Group Leadership

My name is Owen Scott Muir, M.D. and I am a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist practicing in New York City. The current utilization of prior authorization by major payers has been deeply discriminatory it’s impacts on patients with psychiatric conditions. I do not believe the prior authorization has a role in medical care in America with our current fee-for-service and medical loss ratio driven health system. Prior authorization is used extensively, to further the financial aims of bad actors like United healthcare, and their optum subdivision, and there seems to be no limit to what they will consider an opportunity to game the system using prior authorization. I will provide a few examples from just the past few weeks: a patient in our practice, who has been stable for many years on a medication that went generic, vilazodone, became mandated by carelonrx, a subsidiary of anthem, it’s self a subsidiary of CVS Caremark, to submit a prior authorization to continue that medication, unless a preferred medication— in this case, vorioxetine— was prescribed to the patient. There is no medical justification for this recommendation, and there is also no financial rationale that made sense. The co-pay on the on patent medication is $140 a month. The cost of the generic medication that patient was currently taking what is $30 a month when purchased from a cost plus pharmacy. The only rationale for this prior authorization requirement was to increase kickbacks at cost to the patient, and her employer. Similarly, I had a medication for myself Prescribed by my physician for many years suddenly be subject to prior authorization requirements despite being a $15 generic medication. The prior authorization was performed by my physicians office, at which time I was told there is a 15 day quantity limit on a once daily medication, and that if I wanted to get the entire month supply, I would have to use a coupon, another opportunity for a pharmacy benefit manager kick back. It’s about the kickbacks. It’s always about the kickbacks. Prior authorization is used to game the system, so that more rebates flow back to payers, at more cost to consumers. This is racketeering. No Medicare advantage plans should exist. No prior authorization should be allowed. If we are not going to have physicians in control of medicine, it certainly shouldn’t be pharmacy benefit managers. I could go on and on, but I will state unequivocally: prior authorization is used to harm, patience, harm, physicians, and her medical care, no benefit to the finances of either our nation, or our employers. It’s certainly not benefiting our citizens.

I have watched as hundreds of submissions for the coverage of transcranial Magnetic stimulation treatment for psychiatric patients have been routinely denied on the basis of faulty prior authorization requirements, based on unethical request from insurance companies to subject human subjects to need this experimentation in order to justify their financial obligations.

FDA cleared and approved treatments are routinely denied based on spurious criteria, and is worse and more unequal in mental health care than physical health care, which is a violation of the accountable care act.

Prior authorization is routinely used to violate the fiduciary duty that employers have to their plan members as planned sponsors under the combined appropriations act of 2021.

As ProPublica has recently documented, there is a systematic pattern of violation of rules, regarding medical practice, again implemented through the reckless and dangerous use of prior authorization for the financial benefit of bad faith actors.

Putting these companies in charge of Medicare benefits and calling it, Medicare advantage is deeply disingenuous and harmful to the body, politic and the physical bodies and minds of American citizens.

This needs to be stopped. It’s harmful to patients it’s harmful budgets. And it’s a gross distortion of any appropriate use of the mechanism intended to protect us from bad actors.

This needs to be stopped.

Often, my patients must postpone care due to seemingly arbitrary denials, which are overturned on appeal but at considerable time and expense to the provider; delays in making a determination; piecemeal approvals requiring the provider to repeatedly resubmit the same requests; and payment denials for lack of authorization even when it was properly obtained.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly patients and providers must be able to appeal any modification the payer makes to the request if they feel it was made in error.

I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, and the patient’s prior authorization decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. Additionally, a study from HHS’ Office of the Inspector General found that capitated payment models such as those under MA can encourage MAOs to deny prior authorization claims, including claims that would otherwise not be denied under traditional Medicare. My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care.

comment:
Advancing Interoperability

Prior Authorization Requirements, Documentation, and Decision (PARDD) API

Time Frames - Prior authorizations are a keystone of continuity of care. The current manual process of conducting prior authorizations significantly slows down patient care. In a recent American Medical Association study, nearly two-thirds of physicians reported a delay of at least one business day for prior authorization decisions from insurers, while more than a quarter have waited three business days or longer. Providers report that delays in patient care can actually lead to patients abandoning a recommended course of treatment, negatively impacting patient care.

To enhance continuity of care, we recommend a turnaround time of 48 hours for expedited requests based on the technological capabilities of FHIR and the capacity to bundle all relevant clinical information together for adjudication. Similarly, we believe standard requests be returned no later than 4 business days, as FHIR is able to support real-time determinations succinctly.

Limiting a turnaround time to 4 business days will reduce the prior authorization burden for providers and improve outcomes as it will increase the likelihood of patients following through with their intended care. This will help move CMS towards its goal of value -based care.

Moreover, state legislatures on average have prior authorization requirements of 48 hours for urgent requests, and 5 days for non-urgent requests. Aligning with state legislatures would allow for a more seamless and favorable transition.

Supporting Greater Use of the HIPAA X12 278 Standard Through Automation - In our experience of leveraging FHIR for the electronic prior authorization framework, we have demonstrated that FHIR alone can deliver real-time responses for all prior authorization requests by leveraging Clinical Quality Language (CQL). FHIR is also able to combine API resources, package and transfer payloads between two remote parties. FHIR enables the ability to adjudicate clinical data in addition to the administrative data.

A document-driven EDI standard that captures a rigid set of information and uses separate protocols to transfer remote payloads will not support real-time determinations.
Adoption of the X12 278 standard by payers is less than 14% because it is incapable of returning a medical necessity determination, meaning it can only return decisions based on payment allowances. Additionally, payers feel the burden of coupling the HIPAA requirement with FHIR APIs. Payers have raised concern that HIPAA requirements are an unnecessary burden.

There is lack of X12 vendor support for provider systems, inconsistent use of data content from the transaction, and lack of an attachment standard to submit required medical documentation, we believe that FHIR alone would offer far more robust, real-time determination for the PARDD API. The X12 278 has not driven the industry well towards automation and it remains an industry blocker to be overcome. FHIR is specifically built towards automation, and hence for total automation, FHIR is needed.

Reason for Denial of Prior Authorization - We support the requirement of payers to specify the reason for denial. Disclosing the reason for a denial is informative and educative; it will demystify the determination process, leading to greater transparency around whether a decision is based on administrative, reimbursement of medical necessity rules. Additionally, many payers already communicate denial reasons and that such communication processes can easily be implemented and supported via FHIR.

Implementation of Real-time Determination - Real-time determination benefits patients, providers and payers, demonstrably resulting in not just efficiencies and cost savings, but also continuity of care and enhanced outcomes.

Therefore, Smile recommends that payers implement real-time determination by January 1, 2026 (for Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities, by the rating period beginning on or after January 1, 2026, and for QHP issuers on the FFEs, for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026).

To maximize interoperability among provider and payer stakeholders, we ask that CMS mandate the Da Vinci Burden Reduction IGs (CRD, DTR and PAS), as it is the only published FHIR-based interoperability standard that exists. By establishing a common framework, payers and providers will be able to communicate and exchange data in real time.
We recommend that payers leverage the Da Vinci Documentation Templates and Rules IG which specifies how payers can codify their rules in Clinical Quality Language to enable real-time determination. Additionally, we believe that January 1, 2026 is sufficient time for plans to codify their rules using CQL to support real-time decisioning.

comment:

This rule is a step in the right direction, but additional major reforms need to be made to correct the problem of insurance companies putting profit above patients.

While I support CMS’ efforts overall, I urge the agency to see how arbitrary denials have a direct impact on the quality and overall benefits of essential medical services provided by physical therapists. PTs and other providers are continually experiencing more demanding, complicated, and burdensome utilization reduction polices. Often, my patients must postpone care due to seemingly arbitrary denials, which are overturned on appeal but at considerable time and expense to the provider; delays in making a determination; piecemeal approvals requiring the provider to repeatedly resubmit the same requests; and payment denials for lack of authorization even when it was properly obtained.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly patients and providers must be able to appeal any modification the payer makes to the request if they feel it was made in error.

I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, and the patient’s prior authorization decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. Additionally, a study from HHS’ Office of the Inspector General found that capitated payment models such as those under MA can encourage MAOs to deny prior authorization claims, including claims that would otherwise not be denied under traditional Medicare. My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care.

Access Hospitals in the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program



Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:



I am a physical therapist in private practice who has 20 years of experience providing therapy services to Medicare patients. I specialize in post operative rehabilitation. For these patients, delays in care or denial of medically necessary services means poorer outcomes. For providers like me, avoidable administrative burden means that instead of providing care to patients, I am spending time and resources on inefficient paperwork.

I want to thank CMS for its proposal to streamline administrative burden by establishing an automated prior authorization process. Reducing the number of times and how long it will take to process authorization requests is a welcome change. The proposed changes will address avoidable delays in patient care, achieve better health outcomes, and improve the care experience across providers, patients, and caregivers by significantly reducing wait times and increasing transparency around decisions.

In my experience, delays in care means that patients either don’t achieve optimal outcomes or it takes more visits overall; either of those options ends up costing the system more money. The changes you are proposing will make a big difference to both my ability to provide timely patient care and save both time and money.

Your decision will not only impact patients who are covered by Medicare plans but your trailblazing decision will also have a profound impact on how all other insurance providers make these kinds of decisions.

Thank you,
Dr. Preetha Nair, PT,DPT

Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure,
Attached is a document with personal comments related to this proposed rule which begins to standardize the Medicare Advantage Organizations (and other payers). This is very much needed and I appreciate the opportunity to share these comments. In this limited space, I share my first two paragraphs and the final paragraph. In addition, I make myself available to discuss any of these comments if that would help to improve the care we provide to the individuals we work with.
Thank you.

I am a physical therapist and I understand the unnecessary burden placed on healthcare providers when multiple payers each create their own systems and processes for care review and authorization. I have been licensed to practice Physical Therapy in more than 20 states. In addition, I work primarily in post-acute care settings working with our elderly population (geriatrics).

Most of my last 20 years have include setting our EMR in a way to meet requirements, reduce steps, and improve care. This provides great insight into the potential benefits of this proposed rule. In addition, I have firsthand experience dealing with the unknowns of whether medical care would or would not be covered for my mother—care that met all of the publicly stated requirements, received prior authorization, and then had follow up review, appeal, and approval. This is an unnecessary stress on beneficiaries and caregivers which I believe this proposed rule begins to address.

This current proposed rule (Medicare and Medicaid Programs: Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, etc) moves us forward with creating some kind of standardization among processes. This is a good start which will be even better when we 1) Move implementation dates earlier, 2) Decrease decision timelines, 3) Apply these standardized processes to all payers and for all provider types, 4) Require transparency of payers, and 5) Do NOT open the window to payers creating longitudinal health profiles of Medicare beneficiaries.

These comments are regarding The CMS Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes proposed rule (CMS-0057-P).

Please understand what it took for our industry just to adopt the ICD-10 codes and place these objectives in a more realistic timeline.

The register mentions that it does not propose changes to the requirement for covered entities to use the adopted HIPAA transaction standard but proposes impacted payers develop and implement an API that works together with that standard. That leaves a lot for interpretation.

Would hope the industry look at the archaic regulations and requirements that result in faxing and/or mailing manuscripts. At the point and API makes this information available, that should be sufficient. Requiring additional notifications only muddies the water and will reduce the forecast cost savings.

Regarding the interpretation found in paragraph https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2022-26479/p-224 interesting. Today, this information - even for non payment purposes - is required to be sent via X12 837. So if this exchange is information only - just for reporting purposes - HIPAA transaction standards do not apply? I believe this distinction will open up a lot of gray.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. comment:
Regarding CMS0057-P, I applaud the efforts of this proposed rule to address the use of electronic information for interoperability/ communication of information and to improve the authorization process. The transparency to allow the patient or representative access to information is admirable and very much needed. I support fully the effort to provide the patient/consumer with information regarding care processes.
As I am based in a home care agency, I see the struggles the current authorization system for managed care programs exhibit in the fact of the multiple process issues and delays in care that occurs as a result. It is quite common for the care of the patient to be delayed days to weeks waiting on approval of an authorization request. We see the request for more information followed by the denial of receipt of that information followed by the imposed time allotted for the organization to approve the authorization. Many times patients are reluctant to receive services if the authorization has not been approved. Knowing through literature, outcomes are better when there are not gaps in services. Patients are at higher risk immediately following hospitalization, and medications, which are a large cause of return hospitalizations, are at high risk of inaccuracy following a hospital stay place the patient at a very high risk for poor outcomes and re-hospitalization. Any delay in authorization that results in a delay to the initiation of home care can lead to negative outcomes. With the varied level of priority of the request, there is an opportunity to address these areas. As an agency, we have attempted to mark an authorization request as urgent so care can begin timely (CMS requires within 48 hours and has a metric to track that data point). We have received notification that the request has been downgraded to standard and care ends up delayed due to patient decision since authorization has not been approved. We strive to be patient centric yet we have an authorization system even as proposed in the rule that allows for a 14 day response time. In order for the system to allow for care delivery to support the goals of improved outcomes and reduction of hospitalizations, the time frame should be reduced to 72 hours versus 14 days. Please consider redefining the categories allowing a quicker response time in the return of an authorization decision to meet the goals of care. The disparity of access related to the authorization process would be significantly reduced if the response time for decision of authorization request was more timely to the need for the care provision. The idea that the patient or representative would be able to track the timeframe of the submission (available within 24 hours of the authorization request being received, with any status change, and up to a year after the last status change) is a wonderful service as the patient often is in between the insurer and the provider wanting to know information regarding the request. The transparency and the reasons listed if not approved will be very helpful to inform the agency and the patient / representative. Please consider making a decision to amend the time frame of response that is not only achievable but necessary for the benefit of the patient to truly allow the best possible outcome and meet the goal of reducing the burden of the process for the benefit of the one who matters the most.

The Honorable Chiquita Brooks-LaSure

RE: CMS-0057 Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges, Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Eligible Clinicians, and Eligible Hospitals and Critical Access Hospitals in the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program
Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure:
On behalf of the more than 37,000,000 Americans living with kidney diseases and the 21,000 nephrologists, scientists, and other kidney health care professionals who comprise the American Society of Nephrology (ASN), thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule by the Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services (CMS) for “Improving Prior Authorization Processes for Medicare Advantage (MA) Organizations”.
ASN continues to support CMS’ efforts to advance interoperability striving to provide patients unrestricted access to their own personal electronic health records with complete transparency. In our current technological landscape, this requires that patients’ records and decisions of coverage are supported by Application Programming Interface (API) software that allows the open exchange of the patients’ data to the patient and any healthcare providers designated by the patient.
API Related Changes
CMS proposes the following API related changes that will impact payers – particularly MA organizations:
•Patient Access Application Programming Interface (API)- CMS proposes to require payers to have interface capabilities that allow patients to view information on prior authorizations. Also, CMS proposes to have payers submit patient use of this system metric data to CMS annually.
•Provider Access API- CMS proposes to require payers to build and maintain provider access API capacity to share patient data with in-network providers with which the patient has relationships. Providers should have access to patient claims, encounter data, data elements from the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) version 1, and prior authorization requests and decisions. CMS also proposes payers must also include procedures for patients to opt-out of this data exchange.
•Payer-to-Payer Exchange on Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)- CMS proposes to require payers to provide and exchange patient data with a new payer in the event that a patient’s health insurance changes and specifies that exchange occur quarterly for dually/concurrent enrollees.
ASN supports these measures. Data are an integral component of all aspects of our society including healthcare. ASN believes access to that data should be held to the highest standards we have. These measures recognize that a patient’s data are theirs and they have a right to access and share it with other payers or healthcare providers. This is at the foundation of patient-centered care.
In addition, these proposals will help coordinate care across silos that patients face so frequently. In nephrology, a patient may be receiving dialysis care at a facility, have hospitalizations for complications, see a nephrologist in a dialysis facility or in the office, and be waitlisted at a transplant center(s). These silos often use faxes and phone calls to exchange patient information. This situation jeopardizes the patients’ healthcare because of the lack of care coordination and the risks presented in transitions of care.
Improving Prior Authorization Process
CMS proposes the following prior authorization changes that will impact payers – particularly MA organizations:
•Prior Authorization Requirements, Documentation, and Decision (PARDD) API- CMS proposes to require payers to build and maintain electronic systems that allow providers easier access to prior authorization data.

comment:
These regulations are very similar to the H.R. 3173 for MA prior authorization. This bill now appears to be stalled, partly due to the increase in Medicare spending per CBO estimates https://www.cbo.gov/system/files/2022-09/hr3173_0.pdf

There is a risk that this regulation is seen as an attempt by CMS to circumvent a proposal that did not succeed in Congress. If the implementation plan is to work, there must be some assurances to providers/payers/IT vendors that any eventual final rule is durable in order to invest in the technical solution.

Also, prior authorization processes includes these 3 components:

1. Payer medical necessity policy - but payer medical necessity policy is not impacted by this proposed rules, and there is a possibility that payers may add restrictions to medical necessity policy, making it more difficult for patients to obtain care, in an effort to lessen the economic impact of this rule.

2. Patient clinical data used to associate patient status with medical necessity policy - but clinical data quality is not solved, and the ICD-10 codes used in billing and prior authorization transactions may not adequately represent a patient's condition.
ICD-10 is the only ubiquitous vocabulary used to represent patient clinical condition in an electronic health record. For example, in lung cancer the most basic treatment decisions are made based on the differentiation between non-small cell lung cancer vs small cell lung cancer, yet the ICD-10 code set does not provide any distinction between non-small cell and small cell lung cancer.

3. Transmittal of this data - this proposed rule primarily addresses only the transmittal of data.

comment:
I like to concept of this rule and trying to absolve prescriber/pharmacy inefficiencies with the coverage determination/prior authorization process. I also appreciate the attempt at PA transparency of decision/reason to the patient to potentially reduce medication adherence/abandonment issues.

I write to voice two concerns with questions related to guidance on strategy with this rule related to current healthcare workflow pain points:

Concern #1: Inability to receive accurate, up-to-date clinical data through interfaces from electronic medical records (EHRs) for expediting PA decisions. While a payer to payer API and FHIR PARDD API would provide transparency for prescriber to the PA requirements process, the payers are not receiving accurate, up to date medical information like medical conditions, lab values, and/or imaging results from the EHRs automatically. Because of this, payers are requiring prescriber to answer unnecessary questions during the PA process that could have been absolved with EHR data interoperability. So, we still have the same issue of prescriber burden to relay clinical information to payers. Is there a mitigation strategy to assure that EHRs can accurately (and securely) send data to the payer/PBM so that payers can more effectively make PA decisions without relying upon the prescriber to answers question sets through ePA? My concern is that payer to payer APIs will not have the most updated/accurate data to drive coverage determination accuracy, but EHR data would resolve this interoperability gap. If we do not fix this gap, we could suffer from 3 persistent issues: 1) inaccurate decisions based on incomplete data from payer to payer APIs (or lack of updates based on new EHR data), 2) continued delays in PA decisions due to manual, verbal outreach to gather clinical information during PA evaluation that is operationally inefficient for prescriber/pharmacies, and 3) continued prescriber time burden to answer these payer questions that delay the PA decision.

Concern #2: Continued low prescriber adoption rates of the ePA additional question set process. The adoption rate of prescribers answering the clinical evaluation questions sent after initiation of a electronic prior authorization (ePA) request within an EHR remains low. I have some facts and assumptions on why this is occurring. Fact: Payers are asking the prescribers to answer too many questions when this information should be obtained in a different data methods (APIs, EHR, FHIR). Fact: When a prescriber electronically prescribes a medication and it requires a PA, some EHRs are sending the e-prescription transaction simultaneously with the ePA request. This causes confusion as the prescriber does not know they submitted an ePA request at that time and do not anticipate a payer response for additional information. This causes the payer to do manual outreach to the prescriber, delaying the decision making process. Assumption: I also do not know if prescribers are receiving real time notifications in the EHR when the payer is asking for additional ePA information via question sets/branch logic defined in NCPDP standards. If the user workflow for the prescriber is not obvious here, they fail to answer the questions to the payer to expedite the PA decision. Assumption: if prescribers want to use payer specific or switch vendor specific portals, it is time consuming to determine which portal to submit a PA request based on patient plan. Payers must assume that the EHR is building a user interface that is effective and obvious to the prescriber to answer these question sets. Also, payers assume that the branching logic of these question sets are successfully implemented in the EHR so the prescriber isn't answering questions to which payers already have the answers. That is a big assumption without appropriate standardization of the EHR prescriber workflow experience and UI interfaces. Can there be any guidance to the EHRs on how to build this out based on what payers are building so we can align on a technical solution to meet the clinical needs here? Or, is there going to be a centralized portal for prescribers to submit ALL prior authorizations (devoid of the patient's payer/plan) so that we can use a switch vendor to send the ePA request to the correct payer? The NCPDP script standards assure data elements standardization and consist transactional data, but if we are not displaying what the payer intended to the prescriber during the ePA request process, this will continue to be a communication burden between payer/prescriber. If the payers do not have real time access and consistent updates on beneficiary information directly from the EHRs, then the payers will not be able to implement this rule from a technical standpoint to absolve the healthcare inefficiencies associated with this process for prescribers and pharmacies.

The Utah Ophthalmology Society (UOS), which represents 172 ophthalmologists in Utah, appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule regarding requirements on Medicare and Medicaid programs to improve and streamline the electronic exchange of healthcare data, particularly in terms of addressing Medicare Advantage (MA) electronic prior authorization (e-PA) requirements.

The Utah Ophthalmology Society (UOS)would like to thank CMS for taking major steps in modernizing how the American healthcare system and healthcare plans cooperate and collaborate to ensure optimal outcomes for patients and their quality of life. By directly addressing the current issues in MA PA processes and supporting the use of interoperability processes to streamline communication, we believe the provisions of this rule will reduce administrative burden for providers and prevent delayed patient care due to inappropriate PA denials.

Members of Congress have highlighted their concerns about the use of PA by MA programs and the barriers to care these processes put in place for their constituents as well. In the 117th Congress, a bipartisan coalition of over half the Senate, three quarters of the House, and over 500 organizations from across all sectors (patients, providers, pharmaceutical industry, medical technology groups, etc.) rallied around the Improving Seniors’ Timely Access to Care Act (S. 3018/H.R. 3173). Last fall, the House passed the legislation on a unanimous voice vote. Unfortunately, the original Congressional Budget Office scoring caused a delay in the bill’s passage through the Senate, leaving this issue still unaddressed.

We appreciate CMS taking up the issue of electronic PA and are glad to see the many places where language in the legislation and this proposed rule align.

Both the proposed rule and legislation acknowledge that PA:
• Plays an important role in utilization management, but it can be misused or overused, creating
• considerable challenges for patients, providers, and payers;
• Presents a serious health risk for patients when care is delayed;
• Increases provider and payer burden due to inconsistent payer policies, provider workflow
challenges, and unpredictable use of electronic standards; and
• Contributes to significant provider burnout.

• Require public reporting on the use of PA;

• Recognize that health plans’ proprietary interfaces and web portals through which providers
submit their requests remain inefficient and burdensome.

We appreciate the opportunity to provide the physician perspective on MA PA and looks forward to working closely with CMS to further refine regulatory requirements to protect access to sight-saving care. If you have any questions or need additional information, do not hesitate to contact us.

Sincerely,
Utah Ophthalmology Society

comment:
I am a physical therapist in private practice in Baltimore, Maryland and have been treating outpatients covered by Medicare for the last 10 years. I have experienced firsthand the administrative burden caused by prior authorization processes and denials for our Medicare patients. In physical therapy, a delay in care due to lengthy prior authorization processes could result in a patient with a knee replacement, for example, waiting a week between appointments, resulting in lost range of motion, contractures, and scar tissue tightness.

I stridently support CMS’s proposals to improve interoperability and streamline electronic prior authorization. It is critical that CMS finalize the proposed rule to reduce the burden prior authorization has put on both patients and providers. Furthermore, I support expedited requirements for prior authorization, with 48 hours for urgent requests and five calendar days for standard requests to decrease harm done to patients during prior auth delays.

CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will immediately reduce administrative burden and decrease the cost of running my business. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help.

I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly. The result is exhaustion on the part of practice administrators and patients, resulting in early termination of care and poor patient outcomes.

I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, and the patient’s prior authorization decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. Additionally, a study from HHS’ Office of the Inspector General found that capitated payment models such as those under MA can encourage MAOs to deny prior authorization claims, including claims that would otherwise not be denied under traditional Medicare. My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care.

Thank you,

Michael Driggs, DPT

comment: I am writing in support of CMS’ proposals to improve interoperability and streamline electronic prior authorization. The agency’s proposal will help to relieve the immense burden prior authorization has placed on me and other providers. It is critical that CMS finalize the proposed rule to mitigate the unwarranted burden prior authorization has been on both patients and providers. I also encourage CMS to do more to address this issue. This rule is a step in the right direction, but additional major reforms need to be made to correct the problem of insurance companies putting profit above patients. While I support CMS’ efforts overall, I urge the agency to see how arbitrary denials have a direct impact on the quality and overall benefits of essential medical services provided by physical therapists. PTs and other providers are continually experiencing more demanding, complicated, and burdensome utilization reduction polices. Often, my patients must postpone care due to seemingly arbitrary denials, which are overturned on appeal but at considerable time and expense to the provider; delays in making a determination; piecemeal approvals requiring the provider to repeatedly resubmit the same requests; and payment denials for lack of authorization even when it was properly obtained. CMS proposes to require payers to automate prior authorization and place prior authorization information and documentation requirements within the provider’s workflow. As a physical therapist who routinely deals with complex utilization management, this will make my business more efficient and allow me to focus on treating my patients. While prior authorization can have a beneficial impact on quality when used correctly, in most cases it has become a substantial burden for patients and providers due to the immense amount of time required to complete a request, lack of transparency obtaining authorization, payers’ failure to respond in a reasonable time, and partial approvals which lead to a continuous cycle of repeated requests. Often my patients are forced to wait weeks for me to navigate the process CMS recognizes in its proposed rule that this is a problem, admitting that prior authorization has become a huge source of burnout and continues to pose a risk to patients who require immediate care. I applaud CMS for acknowledging this burden that is faced daily by providers, and I know that these proposals will help. I support CMS’ proposal to require payers respond within a certain timeframe, provide a clear reason for denials, and publicly report data on rate of approvals, denials, and appeals. I strongly support the requirement that all payers list a specific reason for denials. I urge CMS to provide a narrow definition of “denial.” It is exceedingly common for payers to only approve two or three PT sessions for patients who had requested more sessions. Because the payer considers its approval of two visits an approval instead of a denial, the patient has no appeal rights, and must obtain prior authorization repeatedly patients and providers must be able to appeal any modification the payer makes to the request if they feel it was made in error. I support CMS’ proposal to give in-network providers access to adjudicated claims, encounter data, and the patient’s prior authorization decisions. I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. My hope is that this process will lead to fewer duplicative requests, less need for appeals, and possibly, lower costs. However, as a provider, I also need access to remittances and cost-sharing information, because I am often expected to help my patients understand their health insurance coverage. Not only does it benefit the patient to have a provider who is familiar with their health plan, but it also helps me avoid negative interactions with the patient when a visit is not adequately covered. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being. I support CMS including Medicare Advantage plans in this rule, given that in 2021 over 88% of services related to physical therapy and speech-language pathology provided by MA plans required prior approval, according to KFF. Additionally, a study from HHS’ Office of the Inspector General found that capitated payment models such as those under MA can encourage MAOs to deny prior authorization claims, including claims that would otherwise not be denied under traditional Medicare. My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care.
