comment:
Case Managers are licensed healthcare professionals who serve as patient advocates to support, guide and coordinate care for patients, families, and caregivers as they navigate their health and wellness journeys. Case Managers are licensed nurses, social workers, therapists, pharmacists, physicians, and others, who work in all healthcare settings including hospitals, insurance companies, workers’ comp, physician offices, community centers and more and each work with Medicare recipients and Medicare Advantage plans. Case Managers are integral to the collaborative care team model, helping to reduce costs and improve health outcomes.

The Case Management Society of America (CMSA) is the professional organization that serves as the authority for the professional practice of case management, representing over 6,000 professional Case Managers across the nation.

Overall, CMSA applauds the work of CMS and is in support of the proposed rule, offering a few additional areas of consideration.

It is our goal to improve the prior authorization process to ensure effective, efficient, and timely care for patients based on their available benefits. Case Managers work daily within prior authorization mandates and experience challenges presented by the differing plan expectations and challenging prior authorization timeframes.

CMSA supports the standardization of requirements across both traditional Medicare plans and Medicare Advantage plans. Case Managers work with patients that are covered by traditional Medicare plans and support extending the same requirements and processes to the Medicare Advantage programs - Case Managers can be more effective, efficient, and precise with coordination of care and benefits across different Medicare plans if this occurred. Researching the requirement of each plan, and finding the reason behind denials, is time consuming and can cause delay in care. If all programs had the same approval process, and authorization is in the control of a physician or physician advisor with the appropriate specialty, patients would be able to access the care needed to improve their individual outcomes. Having standardized criteria that is agreed upon by all the Advantage plans and is similar to criteria used for Medicare would be a great improvement. One burdensome example is that Medicare uses InterQual and Advantage uses Milliman guidelines, which differ greatly and can lead to delays and denials of ongoing care.

Medicare Advantage Plans become a disadvantage plan when they either delay or deny a Medicare beneficiary access to appropriate post-acute services. Consider a stroke patient that is working with a Case Manager. Strong clinical-based data has shown that the most optimal rehab outcomes occur within the first 30 days of a stroke and continue for the first 6 months following the stroke event. Case Managers agree that aggressive rehab during the first 30 days is optimal, and rehab should not stop after 30 days as patients will continue to benefit. A traditional Medicare patient has access to acute rehab or even possibly 100 days of SNF/Subacute rehab, however, a similar presenting Medicare Advantage patient is denied the same services. Denying these patients the appropriate services results in poor health outcomes, a greater degree of disability, greater caregiver burden, and becomes a health equity issue.

Case Managers also experience challenges within managed behavioral health services where much burden is placed on the patient to receive prior authorization and ensure the information gets back to the provider for care. Additionally, individual Medicare Advantage and Medicaid Managed plans consistently bounce dual-eligible patients back and forth, often resulting in wrong in-network providers. These examples delay access to care, result in large out of pocket expenses, or frustrate patients to the point that they forgo the behavioral health care they need.

CMSA supports the streamlined process for prior authorization and recommends further considerations. For Medicare Advantage, new efficiencies should include insurer availability for prior authorizations seven days a week with a streamlined turnaround. Hospital Case Managers find it inefficient that managed care insurers who are focused on length of stay costs for hospitalized patients take an average of two business days to approve transitions of care from acute hospitalization to post-acute rehab beds. For those authorizations occurring after 4:00pm on a Friday, delays of an additional 2-3 days (or more if a holiday is involved) is not uncommon.

CMSA recommends that prior authorization timelines/turnaround times be a maximum of 72 hours for acute settings, and maximum of 48 hours under Medicaid FFS and CHIP FFS programs. CHIP and CHIP managed care entities have delayed authorization turnaround times and should be consistent with all other prior authorization requests.

comment:
Throughout the discussion in the prior authorization proposed rule, the Agencies did not address prior authorizations for services related to emergency medical conditions and related care. Table 4, citing regulatory references for expedited and standard prior authorization timeframes, is incomplete without any reference to emergency services (which can require no prior authorization) and post-stabilization services (which for Medicare Advantage and Managed Medicaid require a decision within 1 hour of request, or the service is deemed covered). This is not merely a semantic omission; when these important patient rights are omitted from such a discussion, it further enforces an already existing preference of insurers to ignore them as well.

Table 4 and almost all of the discussion in this rule addresses prior authorization for elective services. However, when a member presents to a hospital for emergency services and requires hospital admission, or requires post-acute services related to the emergency medical condition - 72 hours and 14 days are far too long for the patient and provider to be waiting for an authorization decision. The Agencies asked for comment on whether the 72 hour expedited timeframe should be shortened. In my opinion, that depends on what situations the Agencies intend to be addressed by that timeframe. If it is not for emergency or related services, then 72 hours or as expeditiously as the beneficiary's health condition requires is fine.

However, for emergency services prior to stabilization, it needs to be re-emphasized that these services are covered and that there can be no prior authorization required, before or after the service is delivered. Medicare Advantage law, Managed Medicaid law, and for commercial plans the ACA and No Surprises Act define very narrow conditions in which payments for emergency services can be denied - limited situations such as notification of the insurer within 10 days (Managed Medicaid 438.114), or an applicable waiting period (ACA, No Surprises Act). While the definitions of stabilization of an EMC can vary slightly among these programs, prohibition on requiring prior authorization for emergency services is common to all. This needs to be emphasized and added to Table 4, because the practice of insurers to deny emergency services based on lack of authorization is rampant in the industry today, and is illegal.

For post-stabilization services related to emergency medical conditions, federal regulations at 422.113(c) and 438.114(e) set a one hour prior approval window in the Medicare Advantage and Managed Medicaid programs. These are not mentioned in Table 4, and this is also significant and misleading omission - one that will do nothing but further embolden such payors to ignore existing federal regulation in this space. If the one hour prior authorization timeframe for post-stabilization services is enforced, it would protect members admitted to the hospital, where stability can be achieved at any point during a hospital admission. In my opinion, the post-stabilization service requirements also extend to post-acute services related to an EMC needed after hospital discharge to an IRF or a SNF, as the point of those services is to get the member to be able to discharge home, if possible. Members who are admitted to the hospital for EMCs routinely wait several days or more for an insurer's decision on approval of post-acute services. If CMS can clarify that the one hour post-stabilization timeframe applies to both of these situations (post-stabilization inpatient services and post-stabilization post-acute services), then there would likely be little need to shorten the expedited timeframe language.

If however, CMS clarifies that the one hour post-stabilization timeframe applies only to post-stabilization inpatient services and not to post-stabilization post-acute services, then the language for expedited prior authorizations should be no later than 24 hours, with similar "as expeditiously as the beneficiary's health condition requires" language.

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on this important proposed rule.

I applaud CMS for proposing an interface that will streamline my workflow and allow me to see patient data more quickly and efficiently. Granting us access to this information will allow us to address all aspects of the patient’s well-being.

My patients should receive the high-quality, earliest care possible no matter who their payer is. I urge CMS to codify any rules now and in the future that foster more open access to physical therapy services and lessen the administrative load that often takes away from a provider’s ability to deliver high-quality patient care.
